analysis.one_liner: Exempts existing backup generators and water-pump engines from EPA air-toxics limits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and died there when the 112th Congress ended, with 2 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would wipe out EPA air-toxics standards for existing stationary diesel and gas engines used to generate electricity for emergencies or demand response, or to run water pumps. Those standards require pollution controls on engines that emit hazardous air pollutants like diesel particulate and formaldehyde. The bill sat in committee and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and operators of existing backup and demand-response generators — hospitals, data centers, telecom facilities, water utilities, and industrial sites — would avoid the cost of installing emission controls or replacing engines. Engine and generator owners in farm states like North Dakota, whose grain-drying and irrigation pumps could be affected, were a natural constituency.

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that three EPA rules governing hazardous air pollutant emissions from stationary engines 'shall have no force or effect' for existing compression-ignition and spark-ignition engines used for emergency power, demand response, or water pumping [S3].
This would spare owners the cost of retrofitting or retiring older, uncontrolled engines, a cost the EPA rules would otherwise impose [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People who live and work near these engines — neighborhoods around hospitals, data centers, and industrial sites — would keep breathing unfiltered diesel exhaust and other hazardous air pollutants. Air quality near those facilities stays worse than under the EPA rules.

drawbacks.text: The exemption leaves existing engines free to emit hazardous air pollutants such as diesel particulate and formaldehyde without controls, so nearby residents bear the health cost of the operators' savings [S2,S3].

By covering 'any subsequent regulation that is substantially the same,' the bill would also block the EPA from fixing the problem later with a similar rule, tying the agency's hands on this class of engines [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings are real but narrow: these engines run only in emergencies or for demand response, so the compliance burden falls on equipment that operates few hours a year. The cost is localized air pollution wherever those engines sit, including around hospitals and water facilities. On balance the bill trades neighborhood air quality for the operating budgets of generator owners, and it never faced a vote, so no legislature ever weighed that trade.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its Energy and Power subcommittee, and neither ever acted on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rick Berg introduced the bill on December 8, 2011, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1,S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power, which was the last action ever taken on it [S5].
The bill attracted 2 Republican cosponsors and no committee markup, floor vote, or Senate action before the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S4,S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of existing backup generators are better off because the bill died — the EPA emission standards they would have been exempted from remain in effect. People living near these engines avoided a localized increase in air toxics.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Generator owners and nearby residents' lungs

for.name: Rick Berg
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, and took no further action before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only Republicans sponsored the bill (1 sponsor, 2 GOP cosponsors), but no one ever voted on it or spoke against it in the record, so the partisan split is unknown.

industries.industry: Owners of backup and demand-response generators (hospitals, data centers, telecom, water utilities)
industries.note: They would have been freed from installing emission controls on existing engines, a saving that comes at the cost of uncontrolled air toxics near the facilities where the engines run.

Existing uncontrolled engines would stay in service longer, delaying replacement sales, but the rules being exempted largely targeted existing engines, so the effect on manufacturers is small either way.
